newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court examines 30 referendum requests.
newsitem.headline: Italian court examines 30 referendum requests.

text.p: Italy's Constitutional Court met on Wednesday to consider whether to allow 30 proposed referendums to go ahead later this year on issues ranging from reform of the electoral system to restrictions on hunting.
The judges began by hearing arguments from campaigners and were not expected to rule before next week on which of them were valid and would be put to a popular vote.
The number of proposed referendums is a record and has sparked heated political debate on whether the mechanism is being abused to override parliamentary law-making.

Eighteen referendums, including one to scrap the remaining element of proportional representation in Italy's electoral system, have been put forward by the radical Reformist party of Marco Pannella, a veteran civil rights campaigner.
The rest have been proposed by presidents of Italy's regions and seek to limit the powers of central government.

Pannella's proposal to abolish the system under which 25 percent of seats in parliament are decided by proportional representation would revolutionise Italy's political landscape if admitted and then endorsed in a popular vote.
A similar referendum bid was rejected by the court in 1995, when it declared the proposal unconstitutional.

Italians voted the same year in 12 referendums and the large number now before the court has raised howls that if all go ahead, voters would face a mind-boggling mountain of questions they would find hard to understand.
Whichever referendums are admitted would be put to the people, all on the same Sunday, between mid-April and mid-June.
Fifty percent of the electorate has to vote for the process to be valid and opponents are already urging Italians to stay at home.
"The only response to the abuse represented by these 30 referendums is to make the exercise fail, blow it up by abstaining," said Greens party parliamentarian Mauro Paissan.

Pannella, whose party has had to gather 500,000 signatures for each of his proposals, and other supporters say referendums have in the past proved the best means of engineering reform, beginning with a landmark plebiscite approving divorce in 1974.
"The only real ethical and political reforms in Italy have come about through referendums," hard-right politician Gustavo Selva wrote in a newspaper article on Wednesday.

Italy's electoral law consisted of pure proportional representation until a referendum in 1993 that showed overwhelming support for change following the corruption scandals that toppled the country's old political guard.
The system was amended to a mix of 75 percent majority voting and 25 percent proportional representation.

Pure majority voting would eject a host of small parties from parliament and, say supporters of the proposal, give a strong boost to the drive for a clearer division between government and opposition.

Among other referendums being considered by the court are one to legalise soft drugs, another seeking to allow salaried workers to pay their own taxes instead of having them deducted at source and one on demilitarising the financial police.
